Chapter: Chapter XVII - Offences Against Property
Section 420: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property
Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
Explanation: This section applies when a person cheats another person and, as a result of that cheating, dishonestly induces the other person to deliver property or to make, alter or destroy a valuable security. Under Indian law, mere failure to fulfill a promise or breach of civil contract is NOT an offence under Section 420 unless dishonest/fraudulent intention existed at the very inception of the transaction.
Key Ingredients: Deception of any person by fraudulent or dishonest inducement; Dishonestly inducing that person to deliver property or make/alter a valuable security; Guilty intention (mens rea) present at the very beginning of the act; Distinction from simple breach of civil agreement
Punishment: Up to 7 years imprisonment + fine

Chapter: Chapter XVII - Offences Against Property
Section 415: Cheating
Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to "cheat".
Explanation: Section 415 defines the foundational offense of cheating. It covers both property delivery and acts or omissions causing harm to mind, body, reputation or property due to intentional deception. Section 420 is an aggravated form of Section 415 specifically focused on delivery of property or valuable security.
Key Ingredients: Deception of any person; Fraudulently or dishonestly inducing delivery of property OR intentionally inducing an act/omission; Harm or likelihood of harm in body, mind, reputation, or property
Punishment: Defined here; punished under Section 417 (up to 1 year imprisonment or fine or both)

Chapter: Part III - Of Registrable Documents
Section 17: Documents of which registration is compulsory
The following documents shall be registered: (a) instruments of gift of immovable property; (b) other non-testamentary instruments which purport or operate to create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish any right, title or interest of value one hundred rupees and upwards, to or in immovable property; (c) non-testamentary instruments which acknowledge receipt of consideration; (d) leases of immovable property from year to year, or for any term exceeding one year, or reserving a yearly rent...
Explanation: Section 17 makes registration legally mandatory for key property documents including sale deeds, gifts of immovable property, leases exceeding one year, and non-testamentary instruments transferring rights valued at ₹100 or more. Under Section 49, an unregistered document requiring registration cannot affect the immovable property or be received as evidence of the transaction.
Key Ingredients: Gifts of immovable property; Instruments creating or extinguishing rights in immovable property exceeding ₹100; Leases from year to year or exceeding 1 year; Contracts to transfer for consideration (Section 17(1A))

Chapter: Chapter XXXIII - Provisions as to Bail and Bonds
Section 438: Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest (Anticipatory Bail)
Where any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section that in the event of such arrest he shall be released on bail.
Explanation: Anticipatory bail is pre-arrest protection granted by a Sessions Court or High Court when an individual genuinely apprehends arrest for a non-bailable offence. The court evaluates the nature of the accusation, antecedents of the applicant, flight risk, and whether the accusation is made with the object of injuring or humiliating the applicant. Transitioned to Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023.
Key Ingredients: Reason to believe arrest is imminent for a non-bailable offence; Jurisdiction lies with Court of Session or High Court; Court considers nature of accusation, criminal history, and flight risk; Interim protective directions can be issued with conditions

documents.publicationRef: India Code (Constitution of India - Section Article 21)
documents.rawText:
Chapter: Part III - Fundamental Rights
Section Article 21: Protection of life and personal liberty
No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
Explanation: Article 21 is the golden cornerstone of Indian Constitutional Law. Through expansive judicial interpretations by the Supreme Court (Maneka Gandhi, Francis Coralie, Puttaswamy), 'Life' means life with human dignity, encompassing the right to privacy, clean environment, speedy trial, livelihood, and legal aid. 'Procedure established by law' must be just, fair, and reasonable.
Key Ingredients: Universal protection to both citizens and non-citizens; Expansive meaning: dignity, privacy, health, fair trial; Procedure established by law must be fair, just, and reasonable (substantive due process)

Chapter: Chapter XI - Offences
Section 66A: Punishment for sending offensive messages through communication service, etc.
Any person who sends, by means of a computer resource or a communication device,- (a) any information that is grossly offensive or has menacing character; or (b) any information which he knows to be false, but for the purpose of causing annoyance, inconvenience, danger, obstruction, insult, injury, criminal intimidation, enmity, hatred or ill will...
Explanation: IMPORTANT LEGAL NOTE: Section 66A of the IT Act was STRUCK DOWN as UNCONSTITUTIONAL in its entirety by the Supreme Court of India in the landmark case of Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1 for violating Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech) due to vagueness and overbreadth. It is NO LONGER ENFORCEABLE law. Continued police registration under 66A was strictly condemned by the Supreme Court in 2021.
Key Ingredients: Struck down by Supreme Court of India on 24 March 2015; Violated Freedom of Speech and Expression under Article 19(1)(a); No prosecution can be initiated or sustained under this section

documents.officialTitle: State of Maharashtra v. Rajesh Shah
documents.collectionLabel: Supreme Court & High Court Verified Precedents
documents.rawText:
[1] CASE: State of Maharashtra v. Rajesh Shah ((2020) 5 SCC 123)
Court: Supreme Court of India | Bench: Division Bench (Hon’ble Supreme Court) | Date: 15 Jan 2020

[2] SUMMARY OF RULING:
The Supreme Court examined the essential ingredients of Section 420 of the IPC and held that mere breach of contract does not automatically constitute cheating. The Court reiterated that dishonest intention at the time of making the promise is a sine qua non (indispensable requirement) for an offence under Section 420.

[3] VERBATIM EXCERPT & HOLDINGS:
It is well settled that in order to establish an offence under Section 420 IPC, the prosecution must show that there was a dishonest intention right at the time of making the representation or promise. Mere inability of the accused to fulfill a subsequent promise does not turn a civil transaction into a criminal offence of cheating.
1. Dishonest intention at the time of inducement is essential.
2. A mere breach of contract is not enough to attract Section 420 IPC.
3. The facts must show cheating and dishonest inducement from the inception.
4. Each case must be examined on its own facts rather than mechanical summoning.
5. The Court considered earlier precedents on the distinction between civil dispute and criminal cheating.

[4] STATUTORY PROVISIONS & AUTHORITIES CITED:
Sections Discussed: IPC Section 420, IPC Section 415, CrPC Section 482. Cited Precedents: Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar (2000) 4 SCC 168, V.Y. Jose v. State of Gujarat (2009) 3 SCC 78.

documents.officialTitle: K. B. Saha and Sons v. Development Consultant Ltd
documents.collectionLabel: Supreme Court & High Court Verified Precedents
documents.rawText:
[1] CASE: K. B. Saha and Sons v. Development Consultant Ltd ((2016) 8 SCC 412)
Court: Supreme Court of India | Bench: Hon’ble Supreme Court of India | Date: 08 Aug 2016

[2] SUMMARY OF RULING:
The Supreme Court laid down landmark principles regarding the evidentiary value of unregistered documents. An unregistered lease deed requiring compulsory registration under Section 17 cannot be received as evidence of any transaction affecting the property, though it may be received for collateral purposes not affecting property rights.

[3] VERBATIM EXCERPT & HOLDINGS:
Section 49 of the Registration Act strictly mandates that no document required by Section 17 to be registered shall affect any immovable property comprised therein unless it has been registered. Collateral purpose cannot be used as an evasion of registration.
1. A document requiring compulsory registration cannot be admitted to prove title or interest in property if unregistered.
2. It can only be used for a collateral purpose that does not create or extinguish right or title.
3. A lease for more than 1 year cannot be proved by an unregistered agreement.

[4] STATUTORY PROVISIONS & AUTHORITIES CITED:
Sections Discussed: Registration Act 1908 Section 17, Registration Act 1908 Section 49, Transfer of Property Act Section 107. Cited Precedents: Rana Vidya Bhushan Singh v. Ratiram (1969) 1 UJ 86 (SC).

documents.officialTitle: Vineet Narain v. Union of India
documents.collectionLabel: Supreme Court & High Court Verified Precedents
documents.rawText:
[1] CASE: Vineet Narain v. Union of India ((1998) 1 SCC 226)
Court: Supreme Court of India | Bench: Hon’ble 3-Judge Bench (CJI J.S. Verma) | Date: 18 Dec 1997

[2] SUMMARY OF RULING:
The Supreme Court established landmark guidelines insulating the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) from political and executive interference, establishing the doctrine of continuing mandamus to oversee probe integrity in the Hawala case.

[3] VERBATIM EXCERPT & HOLDINGS:
The rule of law requires that every investigation into a crime should be conducted without fear or favour and should not be derailed by the station or influence of the person suspected.
1. Rule of law requires independent criminal investigative agencies free from executive interference.
2. Central Vigilance Commission given statutory status.
3. Continuing mandamus exercised by Court to prevent derailment of high-profile corruption probes.

[4] STATUTORY PROVISIONS & AUTHORITIES CITED:
Sections Discussed: Constitution Article 32, Constitution Article 141, Delhi Special Police Establishment Act. Cited Precedents: Union of India v. Sushil Kumar Modi (1997) 4 SCC 770.

documents.officialTitle: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
documents.collectionLabel: Supreme Court & High Court Verified Precedents
documents.rawText:
[1] CASE: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar ((2014) 8 SCC 273)
Court: Supreme Court of India | Bench: Hon’ble Division Bench (Justice C.K. Prasad, Justice P.C. Ghose) | Date: 02 Jul 2014

[2] SUMMARY OF RULING:
The Supreme Court issued mandatory directions restricting routine arrests in offences punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years (such as Section 498A IPC). Police officers must satisfy the checklist under Section 41 CrPC and issue notice of appearance under Section 41A CrPC instead of making mechanical arrests.

[3] VERBATIM EXCERPT & HOLDINGS:
Arrest brings humiliation, curtails freedom and casts scars forever. No arrest can be made because it is lawful for the police officer to do so. The existence of the power to arrest is one thing, the justification for the exercise of it is quite another.
1. Police officers shall not automatically arrest accused when an offence punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years is registered.
2. Notice of appearance under Section 41A must be served within 2 weeks of complaint.
3. Failure to comply makes police officers liable for departmental action and contempt of court.

[4] STATUTORY PROVISIONS & AUTHORITIES CITED:
Sections Discussed: IPC Section 498A, CrPC Section 41, CrPC Section 41A. Cited Precedents: Joginder Kumar v. State of U.P. (1994) 4 SCC 260.

documents.officialTitle: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
documents.collectionLabel: Supreme Court & High Court Verified Precedents
documents.rawText:
[1] CASE: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India ((2015) 5 SCC 1)
Court: Supreme Court of India | Bench: Hon’ble Division Bench (Justice J. Chelameswar, Justice R.F. Nariman) | Date: 24 Mar 2015

[2] SUMMARY OF RULING:
The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 in its entirety for being unconstitutionally vague, overbroad, and creating a chilling effect on freedom of speech and expression on the internet.

[3] VERBATIM EXCERPT & HOLDINGS:
Section 66A is cast so widely that virtually any opinion on any subject could be caught within its net... It takes within its sweep protected speech and must therefore fall in its entirety.
1. Section 66A does not satisfy the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).
2. The clear and present danger / incitement test was applied over mere advocacy.
3. Intermediary safe harbour under Section 79 read down to require court or government order.

[4] STATUTORY PROVISIONS & AUTHORITIES CITED:
Sections Discussed: IT Act Section 66A, Constitution Article 19(1)(a), Constitution Article 19(2). Cited Precedents: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950) SCR 594.

[2] Whenever an accused comes before the Court invoking either the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) or extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution to get the FIR or criminal proceedings quashed essentially on the ground that such proceedings are manifestly frivolous or vexatious, the Court owes a duty to look into the FIR with care and a little more closely.

[3] In civil commercial or property disputes dressed up as criminal complaints under Section 420 IPC, the High Court must examine the materials closely to ensure criminal prosecution is not used as an instrument of harassment or pressure.

[1] Supreme Court of India — 7-Judge Constitution Bench (2023 INSC 1066), decided on 13 December 2023.

[2] Agreements which are not stamped or are inadequately stamped are inadmissible in evidence under Section 35 of the Stamp Act. However, such agreements are not rendered void or void ab initio, nor are they unenforceable.

[3] Non-stamping or inadequate stamping is a curable defect. An objection as to stamping falls within the ambit of the arbitral tribunal under the doctrine of kompetenz-kompetenz, overruling N.N. Global Mercantile (2023) 7 SCC 1.

Chapter: Chapter XVII - Offences Against Property
Section 420: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property
Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

chunks.text:
Explanation: This section applies when a person cheats another person and, as a result of that cheating, dishonestly induces the other person to deliver property or to make, alter or destroy a valuable security. Under Indian law, mere failure to fulfill a promise or breach of civil contract is NOT an offence under Section 420 unless dishonest/fraudulent intention existed at the very inception of the transaction.
Key Ingredients: Deception of any person by fraudulent or dishonest inducement; Dishonestly inducing that person to deliver property or make/alter a valuable security; Guilty intention (mens rea) present at the very beginning of the act; Distinction from simple breach of civil agreement
Punishment: Up to 7 years imprisonment + fine

Chapter: Chapter XVII - Offences Against Property
Section 415: Cheating
Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to "cheat".

chunks.text:
Explanation: Section 415 defines the foundational offense of cheating. It covers both property delivery and acts or omissions causing harm to mind, body, reputation or property due to intentional deception. Section 420 is an aggravated form of Section 415 specifically focused on delivery of property or valuable security.
Key Ingredients: Deception of any person; Fraudulently or dishonestly inducing delivery of property OR intentionally inducing an act/omission; Harm or likelihood of harm in body, mind, reputation, or property
Punishment: Defined here; punished under Section 417 (up to 1 year imprisonment or fine or both)

Explanation: Section 17 makes registration legally mandatory for key property documents including sale deeds, gifts of immovable property, leases exceeding one year, and non-testamentary instruments transferring rights valued at ₹100 or more. Under Section 49, an unregistered document requiring registration cannot affect the immovable property or be received as evidence of the transaction.
Key Ingredients: Gifts of immovable property; Instruments creating or extinguishing rights in immovable property exceeding ₹100; Leases from year to year or exceeding 1 year; Contracts to transfer for consideration (Section 17(1A))

Chapter: Chapter XXXIII - Provisions as to Bail and Bonds
Section 438: Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest (Anticipatory Bail)
Where any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section that in the event of such arrest he shall be released on bail.

chunks.text:
Explanation: Anticipatory bail is pre-arrest protection granted by a Sessions Court or High Court when an individual genuinely apprehends arrest for a non-bailable offence. The court evaluates the nature of the accusation, antecedents of the applicant, flight risk, and whether the accusation is made with the object of injuring or humiliating the applicant. Transitioned to Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023.
Key Ingredients: Reason to believe arrest is imminent for a non-bailable offence; Jurisdiction lies with Court of Session or High Court; Court considers nature of accusation, criminal history, and flight risk; Interim protective directions can be issued with conditions

Chapter: Part III - Fundamental Rights
Section Article 21: Protection of life and personal liberty
No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

Chapter: Part III - Fundamental Rights
Section Article 21: Protection of life and personal liberty
No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
chunks.hierarchyPath: Act: Constitution of India → Section Article 21

chunks.text:
Explanation: Article 21 is the golden cornerstone of Indian Constitutional Law. Through expansive judicial interpretations by the Supreme Court (Maneka Gandhi, Francis Coralie, Puttaswamy), 'Life' means life with human dignity, encompassing the right to privacy, clean environment, speedy trial, livelihood, and legal aid. 'Procedure established by law' must be just, fair, and reasonable.
Key Ingredients: Universal protection to both citizens and non-citizens; Expansive meaning: dignity, privacy, health, fair trial; Procedure established by law must be fair, just, and reasonable (substantive due process)

[1] CASE: State of Maharashtra v. Rajesh Shah ((2020) 5 SCC 123)
Court: Supreme Court of India | Bench: Division Bench (Hon’ble Supreme Court) | Date: 15 Jan 2020

[2] SUMMARY OF RULING:
The Supreme Court examined the essential ingredients of Section 420 of the IPC and held that mere breach of contract does not automatically constitute cheating. The Court reiterated that dishonest intention at the time of making the promise is a sine qua non (indispensable requirement) for an offence under Section 420.

chunks.text:
[3] VERBATIM EXCERPT & HOLDINGS:
It is well settled that in order to establish an offence under Section 420 IPC, the prosecution must show that there was a dishonest intention right at the time of making the representation or promise. Mere inability of the accused to fulfill a subsequent promise does not turn a civil transaction into a criminal offence of cheating.

1. Dishonest intention at the time of inducement is essential.

2. A mere breach of contract is not enough to attract Section 420 IPC.

3. The facts must show cheating and dishonest inducement from the inception.

4. Each case must be examined on its own facts rather than mechanical summoning.

5. The Court considered earlier precedents on the distinction between civil dispute and criminal cheating.

[1] CASE: K. B. Saha and Sons v. Development Consultant Ltd ((2016) 8 SCC 412)
Court: Supreme Court of India | Bench: Hon’ble Supreme Court of India | Date: 08 Aug 2016

[2] SUMMARY OF RULING:
The Supreme Court laid down landmark principles regarding the evidentiary value of unregistered documents. An unregistered lease deed requiring compulsory registration under Section 17 cannot be received as evidence of any transaction affecting the property, though it may be received for collateral purposes not affecting property rights.

[3] VERBATIM EXCERPT & HOLDINGS:
Section 49 of the Registration Act strictly mandates that no document required by Section 17 to be registered shall affect any immovable property comprised therein unless it has been registered. Collateral purpose cannot be used as an evasion of registration.

[1] CASE: Vineet Narain v. Union of India ((1998) 1 SCC 226)
Court: Supreme Court of India | Bench: Hon’ble 3-Judge Bench (CJI J.S. Verma) | Date: 18 Dec 1997

[2] SUMMARY OF RULING:
The Supreme Court established landmark guidelines insulating the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) from political and executive interference, establishing the doctrine of continuing mandamus to oversee probe integrity in the Hawala case.

[3] VERBATIM EXCERPT & HOLDINGS:
The rule of law requires that every investigation into a crime should be conducted without fear or favour and should not be derailed by the station or influence of the person suspected.

1. Rule of law requires independent criminal investigative agencies free from executive interference.

2. Central Vigilance Commission given statutory status.

[1] CASE: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar ((2014) 8 SCC 273)
Court: Supreme Court of India | Bench: Hon’ble Division Bench (Justice C.K. Prasad, Justice P.C. Ghose) | Date: 02 Jul 2014

[2] SUMMARY OF RULING:
The Supreme Court issued mandatory directions restricting routine arrests in offences punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years (such as Section 498A IPC). Police officers must satisfy the checklist under Section 41 CrPC and issue notice of appearance under Section 41A CrPC instead of making mechanical arrests.

[3] VERBATIM EXCERPT & HOLDINGS:
Arrest brings humiliation, curtails freedom and casts scars forever. No arrest can be made because it is lawful for the police officer to do so. The existence of the power to arrest is one thing, the justification for the exercise of it is quite another.

[1] CASE: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India ((2015) 5 SCC 1)
Court: Supreme Court of India | Bench: Hon’ble Division Bench (Justice J. Chelameswar, Justice R.F. Nariman) | Date: 24 Mar 2015

[2] SUMMARY OF RULING:
The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 in its entirety for being unconstitutionally vague, overbroad, and creating a chilling effect on freedom of speech and expression on the internet.

[3] VERBATIM EXCERPT & HOLDINGS:
Section 66A is cast so widely that virtually any opinion on any subject could be caught within its net... It takes within its sweep protected speech and must therefore fall in its entirety.

1. Section 66A does not satisfy the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).

2. The clear and present danger / incitement test was applied over mere advocacy.

[1] Supreme Court of India — Criminal Appeal No. 2340 of 2023 (2023 INSC 683), decided on 08 August 2023.

[2] Whenever an accused comes before the Court invoking either the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) or extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution to get the FIR or criminal proceedings quashed essentially on the ground that such proceedings are manifestly frivolous or vexatious, the Court owes a duty to look into the FIR with care and a little more closely.

[3] In civil commercial or property disputes dressed up as criminal complaints under Section 420 IPC, the High Court must examine the materials closely to ensure criminal prosecution is not used as an instrument of harassment or pressure.

[1] Supreme Court of India — 7-Judge Constitution Bench (2023 INSC 1066), decided on 13 December 2023.

[2] Agreements which are not stamped or are inadequately stamped are inadmissible in evidence under Section 35 of the Stamp Act. However, such agreements are not rendered void or void ab initio, nor are they unenforceable.

[3] Non-stamping or inadequate stamping is a curable defect. An objection as to stamping falls within the ambit of the arbitral tribunal under the doctrine of kompetenz-kompetenz, overruling N.N. Global Mercantile (2023) 7 SCC 1.
